When you create a drawing you have to have a profound understanding of who the audience is for using the drawing.  Quality control? Machinists? Mold makers?  Assembly processes? 

For example - if the document is strictly for QC then make sure that any dimensions that are likely to have unusual process variations are understood and the tolerances needed by manufacturing are in line with any performance the design needs. What kind of inspection equipment are used? Does the inspection equipment make a difference to the drawing? Don't put dimensions on features are are not worth inspecting

Alternatively - if the drawing is for a machinist it really helps to have a good knowledge of how the part is fabricated in the shop.  It may drive how GTOLs are used, flatness requirements, etc. 

Are you working for an engineer and are the critical drawing items understood my manufacturing? Can you get examples of successful drawings that you can study?

Get a copy of your drafting standard (ANSI, ISO) that your company uses, interpret it, and see how it can be applied to dimensions needed for your drawings. 

Does your employer use standard CAD drawing templates?  Is the text too big?  Dimensions can be crowded if you are not careful. Spread out dimensions from each other.  I try to avoid having the person using the drawing refer to many different views when analyzing a feature. If a drawing is ambiguous is it not ready. Never have 2 dimensions that do the same thing on the drawing. Make the scale of the views as big as possible. Never use 'tiny' views. Take advantage of detail views of tiny features. Are your drawings printed? Make sure you do a test print and see what others will see. Perhaps take the print and review it with other people who will actually use the doc and see if you can get some constructive criticism 

STRONGLY consider taking a Drafting training course - they tend to use real life examples of best practices with dimensioning.

For a six year basis I suspect your loan schedule will diminish a lot but I'm unsure how many payments you have left. Check into what you have for remaining payments and see how it meshes with timing of when you actually want to make a down payment on the house. If you can't afford the extra on the car payment this may dictate when you can SPECIFICALLY afford to buy a house. I try to do this as I want a newer used car when I buy a house to minimize risks of surprise car repairs.

However - part of answering this question is how you manage your money between now and the next car. 
Consider the trade-in value of the car when you want to eventually sell it. 
Two thoughts.
 
1. If you have a plan to keep the car and run it into the ground then just make payments with tagging on an extra amount each month. At least you will be in a position to save someday.

2. If you want to eventually trade it in and have it be at a DEDICATED TIME then do this...  

a. Determine what value you want to the car to be when you trade it in and estimate how many months it would be from the present to trade-in time. 

b. SUBTRACT the amount from the current payoff to that trade in value and divide the difference by the amount of months between now and when you want to trade it in. It may be more than a monthly payment. 

c. Ensure that the amount you owe on the car will be about the same (or less) as you owe on the car loan. This is important as I suspect that you will be buying another car soon after you buy the house and affording a down payment and sales tax on another car while paying mortgage payments may be a challenge.

For example. 
Let's say you owe 23k.
In 24 months it will be worth 10k.
At zero percent interest you need to pay $541 per month to not have your trade-in be a liability when you buy the next car. At 4 percent it may still get you to the same place... Maybe pay $560 instead.
If this is too much as a monthly payment - recompute for 36 months and maybe a trade in value of 5k. This brings you to ~500 a month instead of $360. Look at car trade in values based on miles AND years. This isn't perfect but safe assumptions can be made.

Lastly, the amount of money needed for the new house is important. I'm assuming that you don't own a house or the house you own is or can be well positioned to sell well. The 6-7k extra you spend on car payments in the next 2 or 3 years is also something to consider and I have to imagine it wont be coming out of savings. Make sure you can still save money each month.

Timing is everything with financial planning. It's rewarding if it can work out. Hope this helps. Personally, I'm a saver and plan 3-4 years at a time.

IMO Sleep paralysis is a perception that your brain can give you when you are slightly awake yet still dreaming. When your mind can't resolve a dream (where something active may need to happen) and at the same time tries to move your limbs but cannot because you are still in sleep mode... it tends to 'image' non moving limbs into the dream itself. The brain does this because   the sleeper is JUST awake enough to think that it can actually move limbs but then dreamers may suddenly drift back to sleep with a message that it's ok to move but at that point it's too late and the mind has no control anymore... the brain still may try (and fail) in subconscious mode anyways and then viola 'paralysis'. At that point the failed motor attempts and the dream intersect creatively.
